en: Having meditated upon Heramba, Caṇḍikā, Śambhu, Sūrya, Hari, Guru, Sarasvatī, and the best of poets, I shall declare the determination of vowels (Svaranirṇaya), which is the training in the goad of vowels.
From an udātta [vowel], a following *nihata* becomes *svāra*; from a *svarita*, a *pracaya* arises.
A vowel preceding an *udātta* or a *svarita* does not undergo any other change of accent. However, when the consonants *ya* and *va* are employed after that [vowel], [the rule changes].
When a vowel preceded by a non-identical (apūrva) or a low-pitched (nīca) vowel is called *svāra*.
When the vowels *e* or *o*, followed by a high-pitched (*u*) vowel, become unified with a subsequent low-pitched (*akāra*) vowel, that *svara* is then termed *abhinihita*.
Where two *yava*s arise in their proper place, and from those two high [notes], the *svāra* occurs to the north; this is designated as the *kṣaipra*.
That [kṣaipra] is fixed in either the preceding or the following [note]. 5.105.1–2.
Then the teachers, who are experts in vowels and phonemes, declare that [the vowel] is "coalesced" (*praśliṣṭa*). Those four vowels, when impelled by a *svarita*, undergo a tremor (*kampa*);
having understood this correctly, one becomes a knower of the tremor (*kampavid*).

Whatever *svarita* occurs in the Veda preceded by an *udātta*, this is the most extensive *svāra*; it is indeed called *tairovyañjana*. Where there is a *svarita* immediately following an *avagraha*, [it is likewise].

One should know that to be *tairovirāma* if it is an acute (*udātta*) syllable occurring at a word-break (*avagraha*). Where there is a circumflex (*svarita*) due to a hiatus (*vivṛtti*), it is joined (*saṃyuta*);
this is the definition of the foot-division (*pādavṛtta*) as determined by the treatises.
The *jātya* [svarita] is its own [natural] tone; it is called *kṣaipra* by the *jātya*, O Agni, when there is compliance (*śruṣṭi*).
They increased: the *abhinihita* and the *praśliṣṭa* [occur] in "O Indra, lover of songs" (*girvaṇaḥ*).
The *tairovirāma* occurs in the *viṣkambhita*; the *tairovyañjana* [occurs] for the sake of protection (*ūtaye*).
But as for this metrical foot, who indeed knows its definitive illustration?
(12) A circumflex accent following a low tone merges into a single sound; a low tone follows a low tone, and through three [low tones], it attains the state of being high. (13)
The teachers who are most skilled in the science of accents say that when a *svarita* follows an *udātta*, its sound is heard like both *svarita* and *udātta*; they call this the *prakṛti-nihata*.
This occurs where an *udātta* is seen immediately preceding the *abhinihita* [svarita].
In that regard, one should not apply the *svāra* accent to chariot-words; such is the view.

When there is a consonant following a vowel, and if what follows that is a nasalized sound (*anunāsika*), the preceding vowel receives the *nāda* tone; the preceding vowel does not receive the *svāra* tone. 16.
Where a *nāda* follows a vowel and the preceding vowel possesses the *svarita* quality,
there no elision (*ākṣepa*) should be performed, whether the *nāda* or its constituent part (*aṅga*) follows it.
One who knows the scripture should perform a tremor (*kampa*) in accordance with the *svarita*.

One should recognize a short vowel as short and a long vowel as long; likewise, from a circumflex (svarita) it proceeds determinately to a circumflex, and where both of those are seen to be fixed at two morae (mātrās), that is called a short kampita. 18–19.
The *jātya*, the *abhinihita*, the *kṣaipra*, and the *praśliṣṭa*—
these accents tremble where they arise from an acute (*udātta*) or a circumflex (*svarita*). One should gradually apply the grave (*anudātta*), for one should indeed support the circumflex.
If it should return again with a long tremor, that is called *dīrghakampa*.
Twenty-one verses spoken by Jayantasvāmin, renowned as the *Svarāṅkuśa*, have been taught for the sake of establishing the accents (*svara*) of the Bahvṛcas. 22.
Thus ends the Svarāṅkuśā Śikṣā, as proclaimed by the venerable Jayantasvāmin.
